sentences.text: Appalachiosaurus was a bipedal predator belonging to the tyrannosauroid theropod group, specifically a basal member of the Eutyrannosauria clade closely related to true tyrannosaurids like Tyrannosaurus.
While early reconstructions suggested long arms with three large fingers, current understanding indicates it possessed much shorter arms with only two fingers.
The only known specimen is a juvenile measuring approximately 6.5 meters long and weighing 623 kilograms, suggesting adults were significantly larger.
Open sutures between skull bones confirm that this specific individual was definitely a juvenile.
The type specimen was discovered by Auburn University geologist David King in July 1982, and the genus and species were formally named in 2005 by paleontologists Thomas Carr and Thomas Williamson.
The only known species, A. montgomeriensis, is named after Montgomery County, Alabama, while the genus name includes the Greek word 'sauros,' meaning 'lizard,' a common suffix in dinosaur names.
Although several bones of the specimen are crushed, it remains informative; two fused tail vertebrae may be the result of new bone growth following a minor or traumatic injury.
In the original analysis, Asian tyrannosaurs like Alioramus and Alectrosaurus, as well as Eotyrannus from England, were excluded from the classification.

Fossils were found in the Demopolis Chalk Formation of central Alabama, dating to the middle of the Campanian age around 77 million years ago, though the time range spans from the Santonian to the Maastrichtian, approximately 85.7 to 66 million years ago.
